etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English heiȝwai, heiȝwei, from Old English hēahweġ (“main road, highway”), corresponding to high +‎ way. Compare highgate, high street, high road.

Cognate with Scots heaway, heway, hieway, hichway, heichway (“highway”).

definitions.definition: (historical) A road that is higher than the surrounding land and has drainage ditches at the sides
A main public road, especially a multi-lane, high-speed thoroughfare.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, chapter 7, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC:
quote.text: The highway to the East Coast which ran through the borough of Ebbfield had always been a main road and even now, despite the vast garages, the pylons and the gaily painted factory glasshouses which had sprung up beside it, there still remained an occasional trace of past cultures.

definitions.definition: (figurative) A way; a path that leads to a certain destiny

quote.citation: 1979, “Highway to Hell”, in Highway to Hell, performed by AC/DC:
quote.text: I'm on the highway to hell

quote.citation: 2024 May 8, Damian Carrington, “‘Hopeless and broken’: why the world’s top climate scientists are in despair.   World’s top climate scientists expect global heating to blast past 1.5C target”, in The Guardian, UK:
quote.text: So how do the scientists cope with their work being ignored for decades, and living in a world their findings indicate is on a “highway to hell”?.

definitions.definition: (law, rail transport) Any public road for vehicular traffic.
(computing) Synonym of bus (“common connection for two or more circuits or components”)
